summary:
ORBITAL COMMAND is a 3D web-based simulation and AI sandbox that bridges a critical gap in space mission engineering education. While existing platforms focus on isolated physics mechanics or pre-scripted scenarios, they fail to teach the realities of budget constraints, project lifecycles, and real-time operational pressures.
Our platform guides STEM students through all seven phases of a standard NASA project. It features a unique Dual-Role AI: an AI Mentor that uses the Socratic method to coach players through complex design trade-offs, and an AI Commander that simulates high-stakes operational crises. Using authentic NASA data—including RadLab telemetry and DONKI solar alerts—players must design spacecraft, defend their scientific return on investment to secure funding, and manage vital resources.
This solution is vital because it shifts learning from memorizing equations to applying true systems thinking. It equips the next generation of aerospace engineers to understand the long-term consequences of their technical decisions in a dynamic, risk-free environment.
details:
ASEMED is a 3D Web Game and AI Sandbox designed for space mission engineering education. It allows users to design, fund, build, launch, and operate comprehensive space missions by guiding them through the 7 standard phases of a NASA project lifecycle (from Pre-Phase A conceptualization to Phase F decommissioning).

The platform operates on a Realistic Systems Engineering Engine that moves beyond trial-and-error gameplay. It continuously tracks 6 vital resources—Mass, Power, Credits, Data, Bandwidth, and Time-steps. Players must navigate Key Decision Points (KDPs), manage strict margin requirements, and evaluate Technology Readiness Levels (TRL). The engine natively ingests real NASA data (like OSDR RadLab radiation telemetry, DONKI solar events, and JPL Horizons communication delays) to drive gameplay mechanics and real-time operational pressures.

What benefits does it have? The primary benefit is that it replaces the unrealistic "unlimited budget" and instant "right/wrong" feedback loops found in standard educational tools with a cause-and-effect environment. Students experience the long-term consequences of their early design choices. For example, they learn how adding a 2kg high-resolution camera in Phase A might force the purchase of a more expensive launch vehicle or lead to a catastrophic power failure five years later in Phase E.

What is the intended impact of the project? The project aims to build a comprehensive "Total Systems Engineering Training Environment" for the next generation of the NewSpace workforce. It transforms theoretical physics knowledge into applied systems thinking. Furthermore, it develops essential soft skills by forcing students to defend their mission's Scientific Return on Investment (ROI) to secure funding, and it cultivates real-time teamwork and crisis management skills when dealing with in-flight emergencies.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? Our comprehensive tech stack spans web development, AI integration, and physical hardware:

  • Frontend & 3D Engine: React, TypeScript, and Vite, with the 3D Spacecraft Builder and planetary environments powered by Three.js and React Three Fiber.
  • State & Multiplayer: Zustand for state management, Ably for real-time 4-player Co-op synchronization, and Upstash Redis for the REST API.
  • Hosting: Deployed via Vercel.
  • AI Models: Google Gemini API (gemini-3.6-flash and gemini-embedding-001 for RAG/hybrid retrieval) powers the in-game agents. Anthropic's Claude (via Claude Code) and Gemini 4 Archon were utilized during development for writing code, automated testing (373 Vitest tests), and verifying data.
  • Data APIs: NASA OSDR, NASA Open APIs (DONKI), JPL Horizons, and NASA GIBS (loaded via jsDelivr CDN).
  • Hardware Extensions: The web game supports the native Gamepad API, Web Serial, and Wi-Fi to connect external hardware. We designed a Tier 2 "Maker Kit" using an ESP32-S3 microcontroller with 29 physical buttons, scaling up to a Tier 3 custom monolith console with dual joysticks and OLED screens.

How is your project creative? ASEMED innovates by introducing a Dual-Role AI Ecosystem. Instead of using AI just to generate content, we split it into independent roles: an AI Mentor acts as a Chief Engineer using the Socratic method to guide design without giving direct answers, while an AI "Houston" Commander issues real-time voice commands during operational crises.

Additionally, we built a Generative Sandbox & Pitching system. Rather than playing 5 to 10 pre-scripted missions, players can dream up any fictional mission. An AI Funding Council evaluates their proposal based on 6 criteria, forcing players to actively pitch and defend their ideas to receive budget allocations. Finally, the game dynamically remaps the functions of the physical hardware OLED screens based on the uniquely generated AI missions.

What factors did your team consider?

  • The Market Gap: We identified a severe divide between purely physics-based games (like Kerbal Space Program) that lack project lifecycle discipline, and highly accurate but dry professional software (like STK) that lacks guided mentoring and roleplay elements.
  • AI Hallucinations: To prevent the AI from generating scientifically inaccurate physical laws, we strictly limited the AI to a "Language Interface." The AI is stripped of computational authority; all math, physics, and resource calculations are handled strictly by our validated internal Simulation Engine.
  • Hardware Supply Chain Risks: While we designed extensive physical EdTech hardware, we recognized potential manufacturing bottlenecks. Therefore, we optimized the software so the hardware is purely an add-on; the game retains 100% of its educational power playing at "Level 0" on a standard web browser with a mouse and keyboard.
